data.title: South Korea's Lee says speed is vital in AI race on data centre visit
data.description: SEOUL: South Korean President Lee Jae Myung on Saturday (Nov 21) urged the country to move fast as it competes in the global artificial intelligence (AI) race, as he toured a data centre under construction in the southeastern city of Ulsan. "The whole world is competing right now, and speed is vital," Lee said in a public video of his tour. Data centres are a major source of chip demand, and he hoped the success of the project, built by South Korea's second-largest conglomerate SK Group, would draw further investment from global AI companies, Lee said. SK Group is developing the Ulsan data centre jointly with Amazon Web Services (AWS). The estimated cost is 7 trillion won (US$5.2 billion) until 2029, South Korea's science ministry said last year. Operations are scheduled to begin in the second half of 2027. SK Group Chairman Chey Tae-won said in September that the capacity under construction was an initial 103 megawatt by 2029, with plans to expand it by nearly 900 megawatts in the future. The group is also planning further partnerships with global technology companies as the project progresses, Chey said. On Saturday, President Lee said AI investment had mainly been concentrated around Seoul, and that the Ulsan project showed regional growth was possible. After being told that about 900 people were working at the site, Lee said advanced facilities were short of construction workers and that ministries needed to consider how to train the workforce for building data centres and AI infrastructure.

data.title: CrowdStrike in talks to acquire Zscaler, sources say
data.description: Nov 20 : CrowdStrike is in talks to acquire rival cybersecurity provider Zscaler amid consolidation in the security software sector, according to two people familiar with the matter. The talks between the two companies are ongoing, the sources said. No deal is guaranteed, and the discussions could still end without an agreement, the people added. Shares of Zscaler, which has a market capitalization of about $32 billion as of Friday's close, jumped 17 per cent in after-hours trading. CrowdStrike shares fell 8 per cent. A combination would create one of the world's largest pure-play cybersecurity providers as enterprise customers seek to reduce the number of security vendors they use, favoring providers that can deliver multiple products through a single relationship. CrowdStrike and Zscaler did not immediately respond to Reuters requests for comment. CrowdStrike's Falcon platform is widely used to secure endpoints such as laptops, servers and mobile devices, while Zscaler specializes in cloud-based network security services that help companies securely connect users to applications without relying on traditional corporate networks. Founded in 2011 by chief executive George Kurtz, CrowdStrike has grown into one of the world's largest cybersecurity companies, helping organizations detect and respond to cyber threats through its cloud-native software platform. The Austin, Texas-based company has expanded beyond endpoint protection through acquisitions and internal development into areas including cloud, identity and threat intelligence security. The deal would address one of CrowdStrike's biggest gaps in network security and help it compete more directly with platform providers such as Palo Alto Networks. Zscaler, founded in 2007 by chief executive Jay Chaudhry, pioneered zero-trust security, which continuously verifies users and devices before granting access to corporate applications and data. Its cloud-based software lets employees securely access applications from any location. Any transaction would likely require the backing of Chaudhry, who remains Zscaler's largest shareholder. The discussions come as cybersecurity companies race to expand offerings to meet demand for integrated platforms that address a wider range of threats. Zscaler's shares fell sharply earlier this year in a broader software selloff as investors weighed the impact of artificial intelligence, but have since rebounded. Bloomberg News first reported on the merger discussion.

data.title: Cognition in talks for new funding at $75 billion valuation, Bloomberg News reports
data.description: Nov 20 : Coding startup Cognition AI is in funding talks at a $75 billion valuation, Bloomberg News reported on Friday, citing people familiar with the matter. The company is considering raising $2 billion or more in the latest round, the report said, adding that the talks were ongoing and the details could change. The news comes about two months after Cognition raised $2 billion in a Series E funding round at a valuation of $48 billion. The round was led by new investors Andreessen Horowitz and Accel, alongside existing backers Founders Fund, General Catalyst, and Avenir. Cognition did not immediately respond to a Reuters request for comment. The company is an AI startup that develops autonomous software-engineering agents, which can plan, write, test and deploy code with limited human intervention. The company was valued at $26 billion in a funding round in May, when it raised $1 billion.

data.title: Bitcoin falls to its lowest in two years
data.description: Nov 20 : Bitcoin, the world's largest cryptocurrency by market value, slid to its lowest level in two years on Friday as worries over stretched valuations in artificial intelligence stocks rattled investors and weighed on other risk assets. It fell 5.10 per cent to $55,830 by 11:13 p.m. ET on Friday (0413 GMT on Saturday), the lowest since September 2024. It was earlier down by 3.57 per cent at $56,813.68. Earlier on Friday it fell below $60,000 for the first time since July.  Crypto markets have ​been ​shaken ⁠in recent sessions by weeks of concern about the profitability of massive AI infrastructure spending, rising borrowing costs, regulatory risks following ​Democrats' win in the US midterm elections and Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's departure. The main US stock indexes were on track for ​their steepest weekly decline since April 2025, when US President Donald Trump announced "Liberation Day" tariffs.

data.title: SoftBank’s Son explored $1 trillion buyout of SK Hynix, the Information reports
data.description: Nov 20 : SoftBank Group CEO Masayoshi Son recently approached Wall Street institutions about financing a possible trillion-dollar "buyout" of South Korean memory chip company SK Hynix, the Information reported on Friday, citing people familiar with the matter. The Information quoted a SoftBank spokesperson as saying Son was no longer considering such a deal.  “SoftBank explores many opportunities, and this one is no longer under active consideration,” the report said, citing the spokesperson.  SK Hynix said in a statement it has no knowledge of the matter described in the Information report. It added that any foreign acquisition of the company would require prior government approval under Korean law. A SoftBank spokesperson referred to the statement the company gave to the Information, when Reuters sought a comment.

data.title: Honda, Toyota recall 1.6 million vehicles over Takata airbag rupture risk
data.description: WASHINGTON, Nov 20 : Honda and Toyota Motor said on Friday they are recalling about 1.6 million cars, trucks and SUVs over a risk that Takata airbag inflators could rupture. Honda and Toyota both said there were no injuries or crashes tied to the vehicles being recalled, and there have been no airbag inflator ruptures. The automakers will replace the airbag inflators in the recalled vehicles. There have, however, been at least 28 deaths in the United States and more than 400 injuries stemming from defective Takata airbag inflators since 2009, an issue prompting the largest auto recall in US history. All of those deaths involved airbag inflators without a drying agent. At least 20 of those deaths were in Honda vehicles. The vehicles in the current recalls have airbag inflators that contain a moisture-absorbing material — unlike the millions of vehicles recalled previously. The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration said analysis and inflator degradation simulation models conducted by independent testing groups allowed the automakers to act ahead of potential risks. "Honda and Toyota saw early evidence of degradation risk in certain of their vehicles and are currently conducting proactive recalls of vehicles," NHTSA said late Friday, adding that other automakers continue to conduct inflator analysis and testing. The recall includes 810,592 older Honda cars and SUVs in the United States and 790,000 Toyota vehicles worldwide, including 314,000 in the United States. The Toyota recall includes 2002-2010 Lexus SC430, 2011 IS250, 2017 GX460, 2003-2008 Toyota Corolla, 2005-2006 Tundra, 2005-2007 Sequoia and 2016-2017 4Runner. The Honda recall covers some 2013 Honda Accord, 2012-2013 Honda Civic, 2012-2013 Honda CR-V, 2013 Acura ILX and 2013 Acura RDX vehicles. The Honda recall covers vehicles originally sold or registered in 14 states or territories known for high temperature, humidity and large temperature fluctuations. Over the past decade, two dozen major automakers have recalled more than 100 million vehicles fitted with Takata airbag inflators worldwide, including about 67 million vehicles in the United States. Various automakers have also reported hundreds of injuries in vehicles since 2009 from Takata airbag inflators that can explode, unleashing metal shrapnel inside cars and trucks, killing or injuring drivers or other vehicle occupants. Honda said long-term monitoring and analysis revealed potential propellant degradation in certain inflators within specific geographic regions. Toyota warned that degraded propellant could cause the inflator to rupture if the airbag deploys and cause serious injuries. The Honda recall applies to vehicles sold or registered in Alabama, California, Florida, Georgia, Hawaii, Louisiana, Mississippi, South Carolina, Texas, Puerto Rico, US Virgin Islands, Northern Mariana Islands (Saipan), Guam and American Samoa. Toyota did not specify in which US states the recall applies but said it expects the replacement inflators will be ready by early 2027.

data.title: Wall Street regulator proposes to take control of market surveillance tool
data.description: Nov 20 : The US Securities and Exchange Commission on Friday proposed taking direct control of a comprehensive industry-funded market surveillance tool long the subject of cost and privacy complaints, the agency announced. The proposal makes good on the Trump administration's pledge to rework the so-called Consolidated Audit Trail, which the agency first mandated following the 2010 "flash crash," in which Wall Street indices temporarily erased nearly $1 trillion in market value in minutes. The surveillance system remains the only source of its kind for comprehensive, real-time data and information about market events — allowing regulators to reconstruct every order, route and execution for US-listed equities and options nationwide — making it crucial to investigations into possible market misconduct including insider trading and market manipulation. But investment industry and stock market operators have battled over who should foot the bill for its development and operations costs while conservative critics earlier decried what they said was the CAT's invasive collection of personal data. SEC Chair Paul Atkins said in Friday's statement the changes would make the CAT "accountable in its governance and disciplined in its costs," to the benefit of both exchange operators and market participants. The system is currently operated by an organization overseen by the industry-funded Financial Industry Regulatory Authority. SEC officials told reporters on Friday the CAT's current annual operating costs were down about 45 per cent since 2024 to $137 million. But under Friday's proposal, stock exchanges and broker-dealers themselves would collect and report the same data to the agency or its designee, giving the SEC direct control, the agency said. The new rules would also subject the system's costs to annual funding legislation from Congress, something market operators and others warn could expose it to government shutdowns. The agency earlier this year eliminated the systematic collection and storage of traders' personal information such as names, addresses and dates of birth. The announcement confirmed that the Trump administration had stepped back from conservatives' most aggressive moves. The manifesto known as "Project 2025," to which Atkins was a contributor, called for the CAT's outright elimination. The proposal is subject to a 60-day public comment period prior to any decision on whether to adopt a final version.

data.title: Mexican cell carriers facing widespread outages, users report
data.description: MEXICO CITY, Nov 20 : Mexican cellphone users reported widespread service outages on Friday affecting Telcel, AT&T Mexico and Movistar, marking the latest disruption to mobile networks in the country. Users began reporting problems around 11 a.m. local time, including an inability to make calls, loss of cellular signal and problems accessing mobile data, according to outage-tracking platform Downdetector.  • Telcel is controlled by America Movil, while Movistar remains operated by Spain's Telefonica while its sale to US consortium Melisa Acquisition is underway • Spokespeople for America Movil and Movistar did not immediately respond to requests for comment • AT&T Mexico said its network was "operating normally" and that any difficulties communicating with customers from other carriers were "due to reasons unrelated to our network" • Mexico's Commission for Telecommunications Regulation (CRT) also did not immediately respond to a Reuters request • The disruption comes just over a month after users reported outages in mid-October including loss of cellular signal and problems with calls and mobile data

data.title: Databricks in early talks to raise funds at $225 billion valuation, WSJ reports
data.description: Nov 20 : Databricks is in early talks to raise several billion dollars in a new round that would value the data and artificial intelligence software company at about $225 billion, the Wall Street Journal reported on Friday, citing people familiar with the matter. • The deal talks are ongoing and the terms could still change, the report said • Databricks did not immediately respond to Reuters' request for comment • Databricks had said in August it raised $5 billion at a $190 billion valuation, highlighting strong investor demand for companies tied to the AI boom • Founded in 2013, Databricks provides software that helps companies store, manage and analyze data, as well as develop AI applications • The company competes with Snowflake and is widely viewed as a candidate for a future stock market listing • The company has previously said that its Lakebase product has exceeded a $100 million revenue run-rate, while its Lakehouse data warehousing business surpassed a $1.5 billion revenue run-rate

data.title: GTCR explores potential takeover of payments firm Global Payments
data.description: Nov 20 : GTCR is exploring a potential takeover of payments processor Global Payments, the private equity group said in a filing on Friday, days after reports that a consortium effort with CD&R was dropped. Shares of Global Payments closed the day 10 per cent higher. It was up about 19 per cent so far in 2026. GTCR is working with other private equity firms to finance the potential deal, a person familiar with the matter told Reuters. GTCR, which holds a 16.35 per cent stake in Global Payments and is the largest shareholder, said no definitive decision has been made. Global Payments did not immediately respond to Reuters request for a comment. Private equity firms CD&R and GTCR had dropped their pursuit of Global Payments as a buyout consortium, Reuters reported earlier this month, citing people familiar with the matter. The report had added that it was possible that CD&R and GTCR will resume the talks with Global Payments at a later date or another buyer for the company may emerge. Atlanta-based Global Payments is one of the world's largest payment processors. It enables merchants to accept card and digital payments and provides software and technology services to businesses. Its market value stood at about $22 billion, as of last close. The company has faced pressure in recent years from slowing growth in some business lines, intensifying competition and investor demands to boost profitability. Bloomberg News reported the potential takeover deal first and said it could value Global Payments at $50 billion, including debt and premium.

data.title: Hackers breached US Department of Agriculture, NBC News reports
data.description: Nov 20 : Hackers this week breached a system that the US Department of Agriculture uses to send payments to farmers, NBC News reported on Friday, citing two former USDA officials with knowledge of the matter. The department notified employees of the incident on Thursday, the former officials told NBC. While the payments database is the known extent of the intrusion so far, the former officials warned that the compromised system could provide a backdoor to more sensitive information, including food safety data and research on animal-borne illnesses, according to the report. It is not known who was responsible. The Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency referred questions to the USDA, which did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

data.title: Waymo recalls self-driving cars over closed freeway lanes, manual traffic control
data.description: WASHINGTON, Nov 20 : Alphabet's self-driving unit Waymo said on Friday it is issuing two recalls for its robotaxis over incidents involving closed freeway lanes and manual traffic control. Earlier this week, Waymo said it halted operations of its vehicles on US freeways, after a California regulator barred its vehicles from freeways in the state. The California ban, which took effect last week, is a result of a series of incidents where Waymo robotaxis entered active construction zones, the California Department of Motor Vehicles said. Waymo said a statement it filed two safety recalls with the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration on Thursday on its automated driving system "to strengthen how the Waymo Driver navigates closed freeway lanes and intersections with manual traffic control." The closed freeway lanes recall stems from unusual circumstances where a Waymo vehicle may enter and continue driving in a closed freeway lane, the company said, adding it is still working on the recall remedy. Waymo said there were no collisions or injuries reported from the closed freeway events. The manual traffic recall is to ensure self-driving vehicles better responds to manual commands at intersections from law enforcement or other emergency personnel and follows a collision in which a Waymo followed directions from an officer, but the officer was then temporarily obstructed. That update was completed on November 6. Waymo says its technology outperforms statistically comparable human benchmarks and drastically reduces injury-causing crashes. Last week, NHTSA said it opened a recall query into Waymo vehicles after numerous ‌incidents of its robotaxis passing stopped school buses. The probe will look into nearly 3,000 company-owned self-driving vehicles. Investigators want to determine whether a software update Waymo rolled out late last year failed to stop ​its driverless cars from passing school buses with flashing red lights. Most of ​the violations happened after the company said the remedy had been ⁠deployed. Separately, NHTSA and the National Transportation Safety Board have opened probes after one of Waymo's self-driving vehicles struck a child in January near an elementary school ⁠in ​Santa Monica, California.

data.title: Oracle says OpenAI infrastructure deal is fully funded after final capital raise
data.description: Nov 20 : Oracle said on Friday that its infrastructure contract with OpenAI is fully funded following a final capital raise earlier this month. Shares of Oracle rose as much as 3.3 per cent in after-hours trading. • The comments follow investor scrutiny over the amount of capital Oracle would need to fund its expansion of AI data centers and its growing exposure to OpenAI • Oracle and OpenAI plan to develop 4.5 gigawatts of additional data-center capacity in the US, on top of the initial Stargate site in Abilene, Texas • "The financing we outlined at Oracle Investor Day, including vendor financing, is in place. Any further private discussions with vendors are just additional options," Oracle said in a post on X • The company also said that its Abilene campus, where OpenAI's GPT-6 Astra was trained, is nearly complete • Its next gigawatt-scale campus in Shackelford County, Texas, is fully permitted, and the handover of Nvidia's next-generation Vera Rubin racks is on track for the coming weeks, Oracle said • Oracle announced a $20 billion capital raise earlier this month, consisting of about $10 billion in stock and $10 billion in debt

data.title: Commentary: Was Anthropic’s record US$81 billion listing a vote of confidence in AI?
data.description: MELBOURNE: Anthropic, the artificial intelligence giant behind Claude, has just pulled off the biggest initial public offering (IPO) in history .  The company raised US$81 billion by listing on the tech-heavy Nasdaq stock market, beating the previous all-time record of US$75 billion set by SpaceX earlier this year. Initially set at US$83, Anthropic’s share price soared to US$111 after its debut, briefly nudging the company’s value past US$2 trillion, before falling again as investors took profits. The blockbuster stock market listing comes at a nervous moment in the AI sector. Investors are increasingly questioning whether the huge sums of money being poured into the AI boom are justified, and many are reducing their exposure to technology stocks. Adding to this shakiness has been the shock departure of chipmaker Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, following an affair scandal.  Anthropic’s debut certainly sets a benchmark for rival OpenAI, which still plans to go public. But we shouldn’t mistake investor enthusiasm in one company for a broader vote of confidence in the global AI industry.WHAT ANTHROPIC'S IPO PERFORMANCE TELLS US One thing we can learn from this week’s result is that there is a huge amount of demand for Anthropic itself. Strong revenue was one factor. At the end of October, Anthropic’s annualised revenue run rate (an estimate of yearly revenue based on the previous month) was US$81 billion. But the company’s popularity likely also played a role. Claude is one of the most widely used AI tools around the globe. “Familiarity bias” is a well known phenomenon in investing. Intense demand meant many smaller investors missed out on getting shares ahead of the official listing. Last week, Bloomberg reported the share offering was about six times oversubscribed. According to the Wall Street Journal, only about 15 per cent of available shares were ultimately allocated to retail investors. IS ANTHROPIC'S HUGE VALUATION JUSTIFIED? Anthropic’s share price closed the day at US$97.17, up 17 per cent from its IPO price, which values the company at US$1.76 trillion. That’s slightly less than where SpaceX landed at the end of its first day, at US$2.1 trillion. But it’s still a colossal figure, even accounting for the fact that Anthropic beat OpenAI to generating a quarterly operating profit earlier this year (before returning to an operating loss the following quarter).For Anthropic, like any company, going public should make it easier to raise large amounts of capital. That could be important for a company which has already made about US$900 billion in future spending commitments – mostly on computing infrastructure – between now and 2045. However, it’s important to look at how these commitments play out in the short and long term. About half of this spending is due by 2030. The near-term bill over the next 12 months is about US$70 billion, which is manageable with its current revenue run rate of US$81 billion. Other concerns may be more pressing. Anthropic’s third-quarter revenue rose 47 per cent – which is strong – but this compares to a growth rate of 144 per cent in the second quarter. This suggests a sharp slowdown in growth overall. Token prices have also been falling, driven in part by more competition from cheaper AI models. Also on revenue, the company has warned that some of its customers – “particularly early-stage and high-growth companies” – rely on external financing. This could reduce their spending with Anthropic if that financing dries up.WHAT TO WATCH For any company, listing on a public stock exchange introduces much more scrutiny. Previously, the focus on Anthropic has centred on its technology and growth potential. Now, there’ll be a renewed focus on corporate governance. Beyond the financial metrics of revenue growth, profitability, cash flow and more, investors will now more closely scrutinise how management balances commercial returns with AI safety, privacy and social responsibility. Speaking just before the Nasdaq listing, Chief Executive Dario Amodei acknowledged people’s serious safety concerns: "We have always been honest that this technology has very real risks. These range from misuse of the technology by individuals or nation states, to economic disruption, to losing control of AI systems." But he expressed faith in Anthropic’s ability to get the balance right: "If we can show it’s possible to make the right choices on safety and still build an incredibly successful company, others in our industry will be inspired to do the same." Protesters staged major rallies outside the Nasdaq exchange’s New York headquarters and outside Anthropic’s San Francisco headquarters. They called for stronger government regulation and a slowdown or total pause on AI development.OPPORTUNITIES AND CHALLENGES FOR RIVAL OPENAI What does this mean for rival OpenAI?  Another of the world’s major AI companies, OpenAI, had initially planned its own public listing this year. However, it has now ruled this out until 2027, citing safety concerns around the technology. Anthropic’s IPO creates both opportunities and challenges for its rival. On the plus side, Anthropic’s performance gives OpenAI and potential investors a yardstick – including financial performance benchmarks and lots of other useful information. But now that Anthropic has become a publicly listed company, this industry is about to come under even more intense scrutiny. If public sentiment about AI worsens between now and when OpenAI launches its IPO, it could pay a steep price. Angel Zhong is a Professor of Finance at RMIT University. This commentary first appeared on The Conversation.
